title: First Days of School Writing Prompts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart recommends Jen Gonzalez’s argument that asking students about summer break can disadvantage those who had difficult summers, and proposes a set of forward-looking and learning-oriented writing prompts as provisional warm-ups in the first two weeks of school. He maps each prompt type to specific strategies from The Will to Learn—goal-setting to Define Success (Strategy #9), reflection on learning to Unpack Outcomes (Strategy #8). He also makes the case that writing on Day One signals three things simultaneously: that this class does hard work, that the teacher cares to hear from students, and that early submissions provide MGC intelligence without requiring the teacher to read everything at once. The article links a simple logistical suggestion (different opening prompts) to its full motivational architecture.
points: Asking students about summer break can inadvertently disadvantage those with difficult summers; forward-looking or learning-focused prompts are more equitable and immediately activate motivational frameworks like goal-setting and reflection.

Writing on Day One sends a strong signal that this class does the hard and good work of learning—establishing the norm before any resistance can form and demonstrating teacher commitment to academic work from the first moment.

Goal-setting prompts (‘What is a goal you’ve set for yourself this school year?’) enact the Define Success: Wisely, Early, Often strategy from the opening day of class, putting the frame in place before content instruction begins.

Early student writing submissions provide teacher intelligence for MGCs—specific things each student values, fears, or aspires to—without requiring the teacher to read all submissions at once; reading a few per day per class over the first month is sufficient.

Values Affirmation research validates getting students to write about their own experience or values early in the school year as a belonging-building intervention with documented positive effects on student engagement and performance.
quotes: asking students what they did over summer break can put students with sub-optimal summer vacations into a bad spot right out of the gate.
What is a goal you’ve set for yourself this school year? Gets students defining success right out of the gate (Strategy #9 in The Will to Learn).

It signals that in this class we will do the hard and good work of writing. It is very important to get into the actual work of learning as quickly as possible in the school year. Writing on Day One sends a strong message.

It signals that you are a teacher who cares to hear from your students. This helps with your Credibility. It also helps with Belonging, as any time you get students writing about their own experience or the things they value, you’re tapping into the demonstrated power of Values Affirmation interventions.
Give yourself permission to read a few per class period per day in the first month of school and to connect with the students once you’ve read them.
